extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and informed citizens studying public opinion, political theory, and democratic practice
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of the nature, limits, and ideal role of public opinion in democratic society, including how publics form alignments and how crises and problems arise. The text provides conceptual criteria for when and how public opinion can effectively act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between specific and general opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific opinions are particular, concrete choices that issue in immediate executive acts (e.g., take a job, buy or sell); general opinions are about the general conduct of society and give rise only to delegated, indirect, symbolic, intangible results (e.g., votes, resolutions, applause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: choosing between working for the Pennsylvania or the Erie (specific) vs deciding how all railroads should be regulated (general). The two kinds merge but are usefully distinguished because specific opinions lead to direct action while general opinions operate only through collective expression and delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion is external and indirect
rubrics_metrics.description: A public opinion attempts to control the actions of others from the outside; it can influence actors but does not itself execute the acts—its expressions (votes, demonstrations, boycotts) count only insofar as they influence the relevant actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: one should not expect publics to make detailed, technical policy decisions because they lack insider knowledge and executive power. Public opinion's effect is mediated through actors who carry out executive functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public action functions by alignment/enlistment
rubrics_metrics.description: Voting and other acts of public expression are acts of enlistment or alignment: a vote is a promise of support placing the public's force at the disposal of particular individuals or groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat elections as mobilizations of force rather than full expressions of detailed policy views. Political strategy and analysis should therefore focus on alignments and the actors who will execute policy, not on expecting voters to perform technical governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must canalize general opinions via symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: The making of a common will from a multitude of general wishes consists in the use of symbols which assemble emotions after they have been detached from ideas; the process intensifies feeling and degrades significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: political leadership often simplifies and emotionalizes issues to produce unified action. Anti-pattern: relying on abstract reasoning or expecting the mass public to deliberate technical distinctions without symbolic simplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publics are inexpert, intermittent, and coarse in judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of a public are normally not well-informed, are intermittent in interest, slow to be aroused and quick to be diverted; they discern only gross distinctions, personalize issues, and act when events have been melodramatized as conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design civic education and communication assuming limited attention and coarse signals; do not expect continuous engagement or deep technical understanding from mass publics. Recognize limits when soliciting public input on complex policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal role of public opinion: neutralize arbitrary force
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal function of public opinion is to check the use of arbitrary or lawless power in crises so that those directly responsible (agents) may make workable adjustments by consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public opinion should aim to create an equilibrium enabling settlements by the parties directly concerned rather than attempting to govern technical substance itself. Overreach by public opinion into technical governance risks failure or tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public alignment must be guided by simple, objective signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs relevant for public action should be coarse, simple and objective tests that reveal which side in a controversy upholds a workable social rule or attacks an unworkable rule; these signs must be recognizable without insider knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research intended to facilitate public action should seek discoverable cues that uninformed people can use to align themselves reasonably. Communications and advocacy should emphasize such simple, pertinent signs rather than complex technical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of democratic governance: people do not govern directly
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic government should not be seen as the direct, continuous expression of the people's will; government consists of officials (elected and appointed) who handle problems professionally and continuously, while the public intervenes spasmodically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy expectations should reflect that administration and detailed lawmaking are tasks for officials and experts; public interventions are episodic checks or supports rather than constant governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elections are substitutes for conflict, not full statements of policy
rubrics_metrics.description: An election is essentially a paper mobilization — a civilized substitute for fighting — and a vote is a way of signaling alignment with actors who promise to act rather than a full expression of a voter's detailed policy views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret electoral outcomes as indicators of alignments and balances of force; use elections to infer where public support will place resources, not as precise policy mandates from an informed electorate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule is justified pragmatically, not ethically
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical justification of majority rule is the necessity of providing a place in society for the force that resides in numbers (to avoid civil war), not because a majority is ethically or intellectually superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the need for minority protections and institutional mechanisms (civil rights, subsidies for independent institutions) precisely because majority rule is a practical arrangement rather than an intrinsic moral endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government complements public opinion but is vulnerable to the same corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Government enforces working rules, interprets them and counters irregular force; yet when officials attempt to impose their will instead of rendering indirect assistance, they become heavy-handed and tyrannical—government too can be corrupt like public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional design should favor government intervening to stabilize adjustments and assist responsible parties, while preserving checks that bring public opinion to bear when officials fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: A problem arises from uneven rates of change
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems of society are the disharmonies produced when different elements (population, technology, institutions, habits) evolve at different rates; change is significant only relative to other changing elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy analysis should focus on relative rates of change among interacting systems. Example: Malthus—population and food supply changing at different rates creates a 'problem'; adjusting expectations or altering one rate can eliminate the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education of public opinion should identify actors who can compose crises
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of educating public opinion is to discover and teach the clear signs by which members of a public may discern the individuals or sides capable of composing the crisis and producing workable adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic education and research should prioritize discoverable heuristics to help uninformed publics align with competent agents; avoid attempting to train the mass public in detailed technical problem-solving.
